The Calabar angwantibo, Arctocebus calabarensis, is a small, nocturnal strepsirrhine primate inhabiting the dense understory of West African tropical forests. Neonates of this species are remarkably diminutive, with a recorded wet weight at birth of 26.1 grams [Wwb = 26.1 grams]. This altricial neonate is heavily dependent on maternal care during its initial weeks of life, during which it is carried in the mother's mouth or left tethered to a branch while she forages. The reproductive biology is characterized by a relatively extended gestation period; at a stable core body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], pregnancy lasts for 133 days [tg = 133 days], a duration that is considerable for a lorisiform of its size. Following parturition, the suckling juvenile enters a period of growth and nutritional dependency that culminates in weaning at 115 days after birth [tx = 115 days after birth], at which point the offspring has reached a wet weight at weaning of 160 grams [Wwx = 160 grams] at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C].

Juveniles that have achieved nutritional independence undergo a gradual process of somatic development before reaching reproductive maturity. Field studies tracking wild individuals indicate that the time since birth at puberty is 279 days [tp = 279 days] when measured at a body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This transition to a sub-adult stage involves the completion of long bone growth and the onset of gonadal activity, marking the individual as a pre-reproductive juvenile capable of eventually breeding. At this point, the young angwantibo is still attaining its ultimate wet weight, with adults typically reaching an asymptotic body mass of 366 grams [Wwi = 366 grams], though recorded field specimens exhibit a range from 266 to 465 grams, reflecting individual variation in body condition and habitat quality. The species demonstrates a relatively slow life-history pace for a mammal of its size, and the prolonged juvenile period is thought to be associated with the energetic constraints of a diet dominated by caterpillars and other soft-bodied invertebrates.

Reproductive output in the Calabar angwantibo is constrained by a notably low annual fecundity, a pattern typical of many small-bodied, specialised mammalian insectivores. This slow reproductive tempo reflects the substantial energetic investment required to gestate, birth, and nurse a dependent newborn through its protracted developmental period, yielding an annual reproduction rate of one offspring per year [Ri = one offspring per year]. The combination of singleton births and an inter-birth interval approaching twelve months results in one of the lowest annual reproductive rates among sympatric lorisiforms. When assessed under controlled captive conditions at a body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]—which matches their euthermic resting state—the maximum possible frequency of reproductive events is likewise limited to this single annual cycle, underscoring the species' K-selected life-history strategy.

This modest rate of resting oxygen consumption is consistent with the low-energy dietary niche and sedentary foraging behaviour characteristic of angwantibos, which spend extended periods carefully scanning vegetation for their invertebrate prey. The metabolic economy is also reflected in the species' maximum recorded lifespan, which under captive conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] has been documented to extend to 13 years [am = 13 years]. This longevity is remarkable for a mammal with an adult wet weight of 266 to 465 grams (266-465 grams) [Wwi = 266-465 grams] and aligns with the broader pattern of extended lifespans in small-bodied strepsirrhines that exhibit reduced basal metabolic rates and limited extrinsic mortality in their arboreal habitat.
